text: The Achilleion (Greek: Αχίλλειο, Katharevousa: Αχίλλειον) is a palace located in Gastouri, a village approximately ten kilometres south of Corfu city, offering a panoramic view of the city to the north and the southern part of the island, framed by the Ionian Sea to the east. It was built on Corfu for Empress Elisabeth of Austria after a suggestion by the Austrian consul Alexander von Warsberg, following her profound grief over the death of her only son, Crown Prince Rudolf of Austria in the Mayerling incident in 1889. The palace, designed by Italian architect Raffaele Caritto and constructed on an area of 200,000 m², was intended to reflect an ancient Phaeacian palace and is named after the hero Achilles of Greek mythology, a theme central to its design and decoration. The property was originally owned by Corfiote philosopher and diplomat Petros Vrailas-Armenis, known as "Villa Vraila," and was selected by Empress Elisabeth in 1888 as the ideal location for her summer retreat. Her husband, Emperor Franz Joseph of Austria, had owned nearby land. The palace features classical Greek statues and paintings depicting both heroic and tragic scenes from the Trojan War, reflecting Elisabeth’s admiration for Greece, its language, and culture. She envisioned a palace with pillared colonnades and hanging gardens, protected from prying eyes, as a refuge from her past and the world. Elisabeth used the Achilleion only as a private retreat, hosting her daughters Archduchess Marie Valerie and Archduchess Gisela with their husbands; Emperor Franz Joseph never visited. The German sculptor Ernst Herter created the sculpture Dying Achilles (Ancient Greek: Αχιλλεύς θνήσκων), made in Berlin in 1884, which serves as the centrepiece of the Achilleion Gardens. After Elisabeth lost interest and considered selling the palace, much of its interior was moved back to Vienna. She visited until spring 1896, and was assassinated in September 1898 by Italian anarchist Luigi Lucheni in Geneva. The palace was inherited by her daughter, Archduchess Gisela, but was not used frequently. In 1907, German Kaiser Wilhelm II purchased the Achilleion and used it as a summer residence, particularly during the Easter season, staying for about one month annually until the outbreak of World War I, except in 1910 and 1913 due to Balkan political conflicts. During his visits, substantial diplomatic activity occurred, and the palace became a hub of European diplomacy. The Greek royal family, especially Wilhelm’s sister Sophia of Prussia, the crown princess and later queen consort of Greece, frequently visited. Wilhelm invited intellectuals such as German archaeologist Wilhelm Dörpfeld and hired botanist Carl Ludwig Sprenger to manage the park’s plant life. He commissioned a bronze statue of Achilles from sculptor Johannes Götz, representing Achilles in full hoplite uniform with a gorgon’s head relief on the shield, facing north toward the city, and surrounded by palm trees. Archaeologist Reinhard Kekulé von Stradonitz, the Kaiser’s advisor, advised on the statue’s placement, and the inscription "To the Greatest Greek from the Greatest German" was engraved at its base, later removed after World War II. The Kaiser also removed the statue of German poet Heinrich Heine that Elisabeth had installed. His actions were later the subject of British poet Tony Harrison’s 1992 film-poem *The Gaze of the Gorgon*. During World War I, the Achilleion served as a military hospital for French and Serbian troops. After the war, it became the property of the Greek state under the Treaty of Versailles and war reparations in 1919. From 1921 to 1924, it housed an orphanage for Armenian orphans from Constantinople. Between the two world wars, the palace was used for various government functions and many artifacts were auctioned. During World War II, the Axis powers used it as a military headquarters. After the war, it came under the management of the Hellenic Tourist Organisation (HTO). In 1962, a private company leased the palace, converting the upper level into a casino and the lower grounds into a museum; the lease ended in 1983, and management was returned to the HTO. In September 1979, twelve historians from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Germany met in what had once been the Kaiser’s bed-chamber to discuss Wilhelm’s role in German politics, with the proceedings published as *Kaiser Wilhelm II New Interpretations: The Corfu Papers*. The Achilleion briefly regained its status as a center for European diplomacy, hosting the European summit in 1994 and the meeting of European ministers for Agriculture in 2003. It currently operates as a museum under the management of the Hellenic Tourism Development Company, within the Greek National Tourism Organization. The casino function was relocated to the Corfu Hilton. The casino scene in the James Bond film *For Your Eyes Only* (1981) was filmed at the Achilleion. The palace is located at 39°33′45″N 19°54′15″E (39.56250°N 19.90417°E).
